course.title: Esophagus
course.html:
Anatomy

Pharyngeal-esophageal junction (with upper esophageal sphincter) to cardia (with lower esophageal sphincter)

UES = cricopharyngeal muscle and lower pharyngeal sphincter fibres (has minimal resistance area → Killian triangle → Zenker diverticulum)

Length: 18-26 cm; C5-T11

Cervical contact: trachea, spine, carotid arteries, thyroid gland

Thoracic contact: trachea, aortic arch, tracheal junction

Abdominal segment: left hepatic lobe and caudal lobe, gastric fornix, diaphragm and aorta

Enters abdomen through esophageal hiatus → connects to diaphragm through phrenoesophageal ligament (Leimer Bertelli)

Arterial supply

Cervical → inferior thyroid a.

Thoracic → intercostals, aorta, bronchial a.

Abdominal → left gastric, lower left phrenic and splenic a.

Venous drainage

Upper segment → SVC

Middle segment → Azygos v.

Lower segment → Gastric v.

Lymphatic drainage

No segmental nature → rapid lymphatic metastasis

Metastasis often found in the lesser curvature

Nerves

Parasympathetic - vagus nerve or through branches of (lower) recurrent laryngeal nerve

Plexus with sympathetic fibres emerges from the cervical sympathetic ganglia

Lower third esophagus - vagal trunks rotate clockwise and become frontal vagus (left) and distal vagus (right) plexus

Histology

Stratified non-keratinous epithelium

Continued by cylindrical epithelium at esogastrical junction

Junction btw. them = Z line

Inner circular muscle layer

Outer longitudinal muscle layer

Congenital malformations: atresia, esotracheal fistula, stenosis and duplications

Paraclinical

  • 1. Barium enema (not routinely used anymore)
  • 2. Esophagoscopy (allows biopsy!)
  • 3. Manometry
  • 4. Esophageal pH-metry

Common clinical element – esophageal snd

Dysphagia

  • Discomfort or impossibility to swallow
  • Incomplete = only for solids
  • Complete = for solids and fluids + regurgitation
  • Paradoxal = for liquids and absent in solids = achalasia
  • Progressive, continuous and rapid evolution = esophageal cancer
  • Minimal dysphagia, discomfort with temporary pain = initial stages of esophageal disorders
  • Can eventually affect the nutrition state

Regurgitation/ Reflux

  • Involuntary retrograde flow into oral cavity
  • Occurs with dilation of an esophageal segment → volume of regurgitation increases with increased dilation
  • Reduced in esophageal cancer and important in advanced achalasia
  • Can cause respiratory complications of gastric content speeds into respiratory tree

Pain

  • Cervical, dorsal, retrosternal and epigastric pain
  • Due to reflux or esophagitis (stasis in dilated segment → infection → inflammations and ulcerations of mucosa)
  • Esophageal cancer is pain free for extended periods

Sialorrhoea

  • Reflux of abundant oral salivary secretion
  • Result of esophageal stenosis → disables deglutition of saliva
  • Accentuated by high volume secreted through vagal reflex stimulation

Corrosive esophagitis (post-caustic) (not in presentation)

  • By ingestion of caustic substances (acids, bases, salts)
    • ➔Strong acids = coagulation necrosis → transmural necrosis rarely
    • ➔Bases = liquefying necrosis → can erode entire wall, less pain during ingestion → higher intake
  • Stages: necrosis → inflammation → granulation tissue → scarring → stenosis

Clinically

  • Shock → intense pain
  • Dysphagia
  • Sialorrhea
  • Odynophagia
  • Hoarseness
  • Dyspnea
  • Stridor
  • Later: fever, mediastinitis (→ perforation)

Diagnosis

  • Sample of vomited liquid
  • X-ray thorax/ abdomen → mediastinitis
  • Endoscopy (stopped in necrotic area → risk of perforation) → used to place a stent in stenosis
  • Barium is reserved for stenosis, iodine contrast in perforation

Complications

  • Perforation → mediastinitis, peritonitis → prognosis
  • Laryngeal edema (→ tracheostomy)
  • Stenosis → high risk of cancer

Treatment

  • Corticosteroids → not generally recommended; if hoarseness, stridor, dyspnea; prevents stenosis; can mask

mediastinitis/ peritonitis

  • Penicillamine (synthetic collagen inhibitor) → not yet recommended
  • Esophagectomy with esophagoplasty in severe stenosis and to prevent cancer

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)

  • Normal physiological phenomenon experienced intermittently by most people, particularly after a meal
  • GERD = amount of gastric juice that refluxes exceeds normal limit → symptoms with or without associated

esophageal mucosal injury (ie. esophagitis)

  • GERD = all symptoms produced by gastroesophageal reflux
  • LES - normal length and pressure, normal transient relaxation (relaxation in absence of swallowing)
  • GEJ - located in abdomen (positive pressure), length of abdominal esophagus must be 1-2.5 cm, Hiss angle
  • Diaphragmatic crura/ esophageal hiatus = extrinsic/ external sphincter
  • Esophageal clearance must be able to neutralize acid refluxed trough LES
    • a) Mechanical clearance = esophageal peristalsis
    • b) Chemical clearance = saliva
  • Stomach empties properly

Pathophysiology

  • Functional (frequent transient LES relaxation) or mechanical problem of LES is most common cause
  • Certain foods (coffee, alcohol), medications (calcium channel blockers, nitrates, beta-blockers), hormones (progesterone) can decrease pressure of LES
  • Obesity, pregnancy, ascites, coughing (rise of intraabdominal pressure)
  • Smoking
  • Surgical interventions on the stomach: gastrectomy, vagotomy, Heller operation
  • Hiatal hernia → 50% of patients with age HH have reflux
Type 1= gliding hiatal hernia (axial); when GEJ rises above the diaphragm
Type 2= rolling hiatal hernia (para-esophageal); with the GEJ under the diaphragm and the
important tuberosity reached though the lateral-esophageal hiatus
Type 3- Cardio-esophageal malpositions

Typical symptoms

  • Pyrosis/ Heartburn: most common; postprandial, after effort and when lying down
  • Regurgitation: effortless return; sour or bitter taste
  • Dysphagia: mechanical stricture or functional problem

Atypical symptoms

  • Coughing, wheezing: aspiration of gastric content, vagal reflex produces bronchio-construction
  • Damage to lungs (pneumonia, asthma, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis)
  • Vocal cords, hoarseness (laryngitis, cancer): especially in the morning
  • Ear (otitis media)
  • Teeth (enamel decay)
  • Chest pain: reflux, might resemble MI → ECG and cardiac enzymes

Alarm symptoms

  • Weight loss, dysphagia, anemia, upper digestive hemorrhage

Esophagitis

  • s. oben classification
  • Barrett esophagus = chronic reflux of gastric juice into esophagus → squamous epithelium of esophagus is replaced

by intestinal columnar epithelium → 8-15% develop adenocarcinoma

Savary-Miller classification of reflux esophagitis (only remember grade 4)

Grade 1Non-confluent erosions
Grade 2Multiple, confluent, non-circumferential erosions
Grade 3Confluent erosions involving the whole circumference of the esophagus
Grade 4Complications: ulcer, stenosis, Barrett´s esophagus (BE)

Complications

  • Esophageal stenosis
  • BE
  • Esophageal ulcer + ulcer perforation
  • Upper GI hemorrhage

Prognosis

  • Good, but patients daily life affected

Diagnosis

  • Based on typical symptoms + confirmation with paraclinical examinations
  • 1. pH-metry (pH < 4 for 5 min at least 3x in 24h); correlation between symptoms and episodes of reflux; patients with endoscopy confirmed esophagitis do not need pH monitoring Indications
    • Persistence of symptoms while taking adequate antisecretory therapy, such as proton pump inhibitor therapy
    • Recurrence of symptoms after discontinuation of acid-reducing medications
    • Investigation of atypical symptoms, such as chest pain or asthma, in patients without esophagitis
    • Confirmation of the diagnosis in preparation for anti-reflux surgery
  • 2. Manometry: LES < 10 mmHg and peristalsis
  • 3. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy: presence and severity of esophagitis/ Barrett’s esophagus, exclusion of other diseases (e.g., peptic ulcer)
  • 4. Chest X-ray: retrocardiac air bubble in hernia
  • 5. Barium swallow: presence and location of strictures, type and shape of hernia
  • 6. Scintigarphy

DD by endoscopy with biopsy or therapeutic test with nitrites and omeprazole

  • - Esophagitis
  • - Achalasia
  • - Cancer
  • - Diffuse esophageal spasm
  • - Esophageal diverticulum
  • Functional heartburn = classic heartburn but normal upper digestive endoscopy (including biopsies); without

changes in investigations; affects women more; associated with other functional gastrointestinal disorders and psychological comorbidities; treatment - neuromodulators and psychological counseling

  • Hypersensitive esophagus = functional; gastroesophageal reflux within normal limits (normal pH-metry), but

positive correlation between physiological episodes of reflux and heartburn; more often women; often with other functional disorders (dyspepsia, non-cardiac chest pain, IBS); treated with esophageal neuromodulators (TCA, SSRI), surgical anti-reflux treatment important

Treatment

  • 1. Disappearance/ alleviation of symptoms
  • 2. Reduction/ disappearance of esophagitis
  • 3. Prevention/ complications: stenosis, dysphagia, BE and adenocarcinoma, hoarseness, chronic coughing
  • 4. Maintenance of remission
  • 1) Lifestyle changes
  • Weight loss
  • Giving up smoking
  • Raised position of bed support for the head by 15-25 cm
  • Avoiding lying down 3 hours after eating
  • Reduction in fat consumption
  • Avoiding certain foods (chocolate, alcohol, mint, garlic, onions, citric or tomato drinks, coffee)
  • Avoid large meals
  • Avoiding medications which aggravate: teofilin, beta 2 agonists, alpha-adrenergics, anticholinergic drugs, dopamine,

nitrites diazepam, calcium channel blockers

  • Avoiding stress and practice relaxation techniques
2) Drug therapy
Uncomplicated GERDComplicated/ refractory GERD
- H receptor blocker (Famotidine, Nizatidine, Roxatidine)
2
- Or prokinetic (Cisaprid, Metoclopramide, Domperidone
(increases resting sphincter tone and relaxes pyloric sphincter))
- Or PPI’s (Omeprazole, Lansoprazole, Pantoprazole)
(all once per day)		- Treatment enhanced by H2 blockers in double dose
- Or H2 blocker in standard dose associated with
Prokinetic or PPI, 2 doses/day
- Increase in omeprazole also possible

H2 receptors = antacids

PPIs = most powerful, few long term side effects

Prokinetics = only in mild symptoms, long term use has serious complications

  • 3) Surgery
  • Indications for surgical treatment
    • Lack of response to conservative treatment
    • Persistence of esophagitis
    • Psychological factors (difficulties in accepting a long-term treatment)
    • Economic factors
    • Appearance of complications (extraesophageal complications, BE)
    • Favorable moment – during remission period
  • Objectives of antireflux procedures are well standardized and include
    • 1. Re-establishment of pressure in LES through fundoplication
    • 2. Reconstruction of Hiss angle
    • 3. Putting in contact the cardia with the right pillar of the diaphragm
    • 4. Obtaining a 4-5 cm long abdominal segment of the esophagus
    • 5. Reduction of hernia
    • 6. Prevent recurrence
    • 7. Preserved deglutition, vomiting, eructation

Nissen 360° fundoplication; Toupet posterior hemivalve; Dor anterior hemivalve.

  • Choosing the right procedure
    • Normal sized esophagus with good contractibility – 360° fundoplicature of Nissen
    • Low contractibility and faint peristaltic wave - anterior Dor or posterior Toupet hemi valve
    • All performed laparoscopically or laparo- and thoracoscopically
    • Contraindications to laparoscopic approach: cirrhosis and previous history on the supramesocolic level
  • Laparoscopic fundoplication
    • Performed under general endotracheal anesthesia
    • 5 incisions are used
    • Fundus of stomach is wrapped around esophagus to create a new valve at level of GEJ
    • Valve length is maximum 3 cm and must be free of tension (floppy-Nissen)
    • Essential elements
      • I. Mobilization of fundus (with or without division of short gastric vessels)
      • II. Reduction of hiatal hernia
      • III. Calibration of esophageal hiatus
      • IV. Obtaining at least 3 cm abdominal esophagus segment
      • V. Creation of an over 40 French intraesophageal tube (Nissen fundoplication)
    • Partial fundoplications have a lower continence, which translates into a slight increase in reflux episodes but

also by reducing dysphagia

  • Hiatal hernia repair
    • Suturing of dilated hiatus done posteriorly
    • Use of prosthetic materials should be avoided due to risk of erosion with esophageal fistula
    • Autologous fascia lata plastic surgery is cheaper than heterologous biological grafts
  • Post-OP evolution
    • Good, with minimal dysphagia
    • Limiting food intake to fluids for 2-3 days
    • Prolonged dysphagia requires barium transit
    • In case of post-fundoplication stenosis, endoscopic dilation may be necessary
    • Postoperative follow-up based on clinical data, except for patients with Barrett's esophagus → periodic endoscopy
    • In recurrence of reflux or dysphagia → begin with barium swallow and continue with endoscopy and pH-metry
    • Slightly slipped fundoplication in chest (less than 2 cm) and without symptoms has no surgical indication
  • Complication
    • Nissen stenosis
    • Vagus nerves can be damaged by dissection too close to esophageal wall, but gastric paresis and secondary pyloric spasm occur only if both vaguses are injured

Other procedures not in the book but slides

Collis gastroplasty

= simplified variant, which does not require a thoracoscopic approach but only laparoscopic, prolongs the esophagus by a wedge resection (wedge-fundectomy) of a fundic segment

  • Patients with morbid obesity and GERD should benefit from gastric bypass on the Y en Roux loop, as this bariatric intervention has proven anti-reflux valences
  • Performed mainly in recurrences, the Belsey Mark IV operation consists of a partial fundoplication by thoracic approach, the advantage being maximum in recurrences because it avoids passing through the subphrenic adhesion area with reduced risk of splenic and esophageal damage
  • Endoscopic application techniques are part of the range of endoscopic surgery through natural orifices (NOTES- Natural Orifice Transluminal Endoscopic Surgery) and are tempting for the patient, but the medium and long term results are clearly inferior to the surgical background. More well known is the TIF technique which uses a device called Esophyx which is mounted on an endoscope and performs a "full-thickness" partial valve fixed with a type of plastic T-shaped buttons. It is an expensive, laborious technique with inferior results to laparoscopic fundoplications
  • Endoluminal gastroplication
  • Endoscopic procedures → Stretta procedure
  • Radiofrequency energy delivery catheter and guidewire
  • Ethylene-vinyl alcohol injection

Esophageal diverticuli

= dilations at different levels of the esophagus, which communicate directly with esophageal lumen

Cervical
Diverticuli
= Zenker
diverticulum		- Men over 60
- Often together with hiatal hernias
- Due to dyssynergy of cricopharyngeal muscle which contracts prematurely, creating a
pressure zone at pharyngo-esophag. junction level → distal wall becomes thinner
→ protrusion through mucosa and submucosa
- Clinically: dysphagia, typical gurgling noise at liquid ingestion, undigested foods, stasis and
decomposition → foetor ex ore (halitosis) and appearance of diverticulitis
- Diagnosis: latero-cervical formation of variable volume, contrast X-ray/ Ba swallow (additional
image left paravertebral region), esophagoscopy (biopsy)
- Complications of diverticulitis: hemorrhage, perforation, malignization, nocturnal aspiration
pneumonia, lung abscess, bi-tonal voice
- Treatment
- Surgical always indicated - dissection of diverticular neck, resection, wall reconstructed by
two-layer suture
- Cricopharyngeal myotomy mandatory to prevent recurrence
Parabronchial
diverticuli		- Retro scarring retraction of a mediastinal lymph node adhering to the esophageal wall
- In general after infection with Koch bacillus
- All the normal layers
- Mostly asymptomatic, can cause coughing by adherence to trachea, dysphagia
- Complications: hemorrhage, perforation, pericarditis, pleuresia, esobronchial fistula
- Treatment: surgical resection in symptomatic p., suture of fistula, interposition of healthy
tissue to prevent recurrency
Epiphrenic
diverticuli		- Located immediately above diaphragm (larger)
- Due to esophageal dyskinesia
- Frequently associated with hiatal hernia and achalasia
- Clinically: dysphagia, intermittent regurgitation, postprandial pressure, high epigastric
pressure
- Diagnosis: dysphagia with postprandial onset which is alleviated after regurgitation, contrast
X-ray (typical aspect), esophagoscopy (not routinely necessary)
- Complications: diverticulitis, haemorrhage, perforations or even malignization
- Treatment: indicated in symptomes; thoracotomy → resection and double suture, associated
esophageal conditions (achalasia, hiatal hernia)

Achalasia (megaesophagus)

= failure in LES relaxation and lack of peristaltic waves

Pathogenesis

  • Degeneration of the Auerbach plexus

Clinically

  • Dysphagia - most constant and precocious symptom; at beginning intermittent; accentuated in cold food; paradoxical; paroxistic, appearing in episodes separated by lull; over time, becomes permanent
  • High or retrosternal epigastric pains - rare
  • Regurgitation – usual; more frequently at night, in clinostatism
  • Sialorrhoea

Complications are related to stasis esophagitis

  • Ulcerations
  • Hemorrhage
  • Esophageal cancer (7x more frequent)
  • Aspiration pneumonia and lung abscesses

Paraclinical investigations

  • Barium swallowing – dilation, uncoordinated or missing peristalsis; Glucagon relaxation test to differentiate from

organic stenosis; “birds beak” at the end; overtime lengthening and curved esophagus

  • Endoscopy with biopsy - DD from cancer
  • Manometry (persistent pressure >25 mmHg) - uncoordinated contractile wave, relaxation is incomplete

Diagnosis

  • Symptoms + prolonged evolution without affecting nutritional state are typical of achalasia
  • Radiological aspect and manometry data confirm

DD

  • - Esophageal cancer - progressive dysphagia, rapid evolution and affects general state
  • - Epiphrenic diverticuli complicated by esophagitis - distinguished based on barium swallow, manometry in

diverticulum is normal, diagnosis is more difficult in cases of associating epiphrenic diverticulum with achalasia/ hiatal hernia

  • - Hiatal hernia - difficult to distinguish clinically, requires barium swallow in Trendelenburg position and fibroscopy;

manometry reveals low values of LES tonus, by contrast to achalasia for which values are higher

Treatment

  • Life style - avoiding stress, too hot/ too cold food, small meals
  • Mechanical - forced, mechanic, pneumatic or hydrostatic dilation has good results
  • Pharmacological - calcium channel blockers (nifedipine, verapamil)
  • Botulinium toxin
  • Surgical - Heller myotomy (extramucous esocardiomyotomy → longitudinal incision of 6-8 cm on esogastric junction, with sectioning of muscles reaching up to mucosa) + Nissen fundoplication in case of hypermotility + Anterior Dor hemi valve in case of hypomotility

Benign tumors of the esophagus

  • Inflammatory polyps or granulomatous lesions in esophagitis - require biopsy for diagnosis
  • Leiomyoma = most common benign lesion, within the wall, stenosis of lumen, mucosa intact
  • Congenital cysts or esophageal dedoubling - lower esophagus
  • Lesions can be seen on contrast X ray - benign stenosis, dilations are rare, peristalsis not affected except for congenital diseases

Esophageal cancer

Epidemiology

  • Especially Asia
  • 45-65 years men
  • High alcohol consumption, hot food and liquids, vitamin or nutritional deficiencies, poor oral hygiene, nitrosamines in environment or food, smoking, Plummer-Vinson syndrome, static/ caustic/ peptic esophagitis
    • squamous carcinoma
  • Pre-existing esophageal lesions = BE → adenocarcinoma

Pathomorphology

  • Vegetative form – can be ulcerative
  • Infiltrative, circumferential forms - causing obstructive symptoms
  • Cervical and thoracic (upper 2/3) = squamous cell carcinoma
  • Lower thoracic and abdominal (lower 1/3) = adenocarcinoma
  • Extends on mucosa, invades esophageal wall and neighboring tissues, disseminate through lymph and blood
  • Cervical - cervical lymph nodes (anterior jugular and supraclavicular groups)
  • Thoracic - mediastinal, supraclavicular and sometimes subdiaphragmatic lymph nodes
  • Abdominal - celiac and small gastric curvature nodes
  • Upper 2/3 - rapidly invade airways, large vessels, pleura, thoracic outlet and recurrent nerves
  • Blood metastases: liver, lungs, bones
  • Presence of mediastinal syndrome, eso-tracheal or eso-bronchial fistula, bitonal voice, Virchow-Troisier’s sign = radical intervention impossible

Clinical picture – 3 stages

1. Onset- Dysphagia (progressive, feeling that solid food stops, burning sensation at
warm liquids)
2. Status- Dysphagia becomes permanent (first only for solids, then also for liquids)
- Regurgitation, sialorrhea, bad breath, hiccup, dysphonia/ hoarseness
- Pain (epigastric, retrosternal) due to spasm
3. Complications- Aspiration pneumonia
- Eso-tracheal and eso-bronchial fistulas
- Mediastinitis and hemorrhage
- Pain due to invasion of mediastinum/ pleura
- Weight loss !!!, asthenia, dehydration, anorexia

Dysphagia = always indication for barium swallow and endoscopy

Physical exam

  • Often normal
  • Lymphadenopathy in latero-cervical or supraclavicular (Virchow) areas → sign for metastasis → FNA
    • contraindication for surgery
  • Liver metastasis might cause jaundice → contraindication for surgery
  • Anemia (pallor)

Diagnosis/ Paraclinical investigations

  • Lab: anemia (iron or chronic disease); abnormal transaminases, PT and aPTT → hepatic dysfunction
  • Barium esophagography/ swallow (double contrast) !
    • Images suggestive for esophageal cancer
      • ➔irregular contour stenosis (apple core aspect)
      • ➔eccentric stenosis with slight suprajacent dilation
      • ➔marginal emptiness
      • ➔niche
      • ➔rigidity
      • ➔irregularity
      • ➔presence on all images even after administration of pharmacodynamic agents
  • Esophagoscopy (EGD)
    • Direct tumor visualization ! , location, type (infiltrative, vegetative, ulcerated) and biopsy ! (histology)
    • Location/ distance: point A = dental archade (incisors); point B = location of tumor
  • Endoesophageal ultrasound (EUS)
    • = Golden standard - depth and penetration of tumor (T staging) and N staging
  • Abdominal, chest, pelvic CT contrast
    • M staging for lungs and liver
  • Bronchoscopy for cancers in middle and upper 1/3 of thoracic esophagus and exclusion of trachea/ bronchi involvement
  • Bone scan → bone metastasis
  • Laparoscopy and thoracoscopy → staging of regional lymph nodes
  • PET-scan

Positive diagnosis

  • Clinical, radiological and endoscopic methods
  • Often found at advanced stage
  • Any patient over 40 with dysphagia should be fully investigated
  • Typical patient: male, consumer of spirits, with progressive permanent dysphagia, long time without pain

DD

  • Achalasia – paradoxical, paroxystic intermittent dysphagia, prolonged evolution; nutritional state normal; barium meal or manometry, fibroscope goes easily beyond cardia
  • Asymptomatic diverticuli – barium meal
  • Benign stenoses - history of post caustic, reflux, infectious, drug induced esophagitis, or radiation therapy of chest; barium meal or endoscopy + biopsy
  • Extrinsic compressions - mediastinal adenopathy or tumors, retrosternal gout, vertebral osteophytosis, aortic aneurysm, pulmonary hydatid cyst

Prognosis

  • Severe - 5 year survival = 5%
  • Postoperative mortality high (mediastinitis has worst prognosis)

Treatment

  • depending on stage (radical/palliative)
    • TNM staging
  • Pre-operative care
    • Improvement of general status (nutrition)
    • Preparation of colon for possible esophagoplasty
    • Improve/ check respiratory function (CT of lungs and spirometry) (thorax involvement during surgery, can develop post-OP problems)
    • +/- Neoadjuvant chemoradiation therapy to downstage tumor
      • depending on costs, perioperative morbidity, delay in surgical intervention
  • Operation
    • Radical esophagectomy in neoplasms of upper or middle third → replacement of esophagus by another segment of GI tract
    • Partial esophagectomy in neoplasms of lower third with upper polar gastric resection (6-10 cm from tumor) → within oncological safety, under observation due to multifocal development of esophageal cancer
    • Resection also involves removal of surrounding lymph nodes + lymph drainage

Techniques → transthoracic, transhiatal, en bloc

Orringer technique- Cervical and abdominal incision → transhiatal, both hands go into thorax
- No opening of thorax
- Advantages: pat. with poor pulmonary status, prior major thoracic surgery,
avoidance of intrathoracic anastomosis
- Disadvantages: risk of limited access in case of bleeding, limited resection of
large tumors, greater potency of local tumor spillage, greater
stretch of stomach to reach neck → ↑ risk for anastomotic
failure due to tension, ischemia
→ Ideal for local limited diseases of distal esophagus (Barrett’s)
Ivor-Lewis technique= historical, right transthoracic and abdominal incision
- Gastro-esophageal anastomosis is located in right chest
- Visually direct resection of tumor, BUT ↑ morbidity
McKeown technique
!		= tri-incisional esophagectomy (cervical, right thorax, abdomen)
- Similar to Ivor-Lewis → including cervical incision and cervical gastro-
esophageal anastomosis (↓ risk for anastomosis leakage)
- For lesions in proximal/ mid-esophagus
- Advantages: wider surgical margins, ↓ risk for anastomosis leakage
En bloc resection= left thoracic incision
- Used for distal esophageal tumors extending into stomach
- Advantage: cleaner oncological resection

Laparoscopic Advantages

  • Less post-op pain
  • Faster post-op recovery
  • shorter hospital stay, more rapid return to normal life
  • - Thoracoscopic dissection of esophagus is nowadays more common instead of

open thoracotomy

Orringer

  • After esophagectomy → esophagoplasty
  • Uses stomach, colon, jejunum
  • Depends on availability (previous gastrectomy, vascular disease), location of resected esophagus segment and surgeon’s preference
1. Stomach= Dan Gavriliu’s method
- Most frequently used
- Gastric tube made from greater stomach curvature (removal of other stomach parts)
- After hilum splenectomy and ligation of left gastric and gastroepiploic artery
- Vagus n. is divided during esophagectomy → pyloromyotomy to facilitate
gastric emptying
- Brought to chest → end-to-end anastomosis
- Vascularization via right gastric and gastroepiploic arteries
Advantages: rich vascular supply, ease of surgical mobilization as a vascular
pedicle, need to create fewer GI anastomosis
Disadvantages: risk of fundus ischemia, risk of post-op GERD
2. Left colonCan be done in 2 ways
a. Through resected esophageal space in post. mediastinum
b. Through retrosternum (only if a. is not possible)
Advantages: longer available length → longer and more relaxed reach to cervical
esophagus, favorable vascular anatomy, close size match, colon is more resistant
to reflux
Disadvantages: need to perform 2 additional anastomosis, greater technique
experience needed in assessing & mobilizing colonic vasculature, pre-op
colonoscopy + visceral angiography
3. Jejunum- Rarely used
- Used as free graft, especially when a short segment of the cervical
esophagus is resected
→ jejunal reconstruction via Roux-en-Y connection can be used
when a total gastrectomy is combined with distal esophagectomy
  • Post-op care
    • Enteral nutrition 4-6 weeks
    • Once normal diet started → decreased stomach size → need to eat more frequent and smaller meals
      • weight loss is possible
  • Complications
Cancer relatedSurgery relatedOthers
- Esophageal stenosis
- Tracheoesophageal fistula
→ poor vascularization and lack of
serosa		- Anastomosis leaks
→ poor vascularization and lack of
serosa
→ mediastinitis and purulent pleurisy
almost always fatal
- Recurrent laryngeal n. injury		- Dysphagia
- Reflux
- Dumping syndrome
- Mediastinitis
- Purulent pleurisy
  • Palliative treatment
    • = are indicated in case of local and regional spread as well as remote metastases
    • Survival time of up to 18 months may be obtained
    • To provide a “comfortable” quality of life in the limited time available
    • To relief severe symptoms/ complications (dysphagia, obstruction)
    • These methods are surgery, radiation and chemotherapy
      • a) Dilation → balloon expansion (risk of perforation)
      • b) Stents, transtumoral endoprosthesis → for mid/ distal esophageal tumors; pat. with

tracheoesophageal fistula and when chemoradiation therapy is contraindicated

  • c) Photodynamic therapy, endoscopic laser ablation
  • d) Radiation- and chemotherapy → reduce tumor size and improve dysphagia (complications:

actinic lung, pericarditis and tumoral necrosis with fistula formation)

  • e) Surgery → palliative esophagectomy with incomplete tumor removal, alimentation gastrostomy

The Esophagus Benign esophageal disorders

Ion Cosmin Puia

ANATOMY

The esophagus extends from the pharyngeal-esophageal junction area to the cardia. The upper esophageal sphincter is located at the level of the pharyngo-esophageal junction and comprises the cricopharyngeal muscle and lower pharyngeal sphincter fibres. The cricopharyngeal muscle has on the distal end of the esophagus a minimal resistance area, the Killian triangle, where the Zenker diverticulum emerges. The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) is in fact more functional than anatomical sphincter. Its components are detailed within the subchapter of the gastro-esophageal reflux disease.

The esophagus projection has a variable length (18--26 cm) extending from C5 to T11 vertebra. The cervical esophagus extends to the upper extremity of the sternal manubrium and enters in frontal contact with the trachea, distal with the vertebral spine and lateral with the carotid arteries and the thyroid gland. The thoracic segment extends to the esophageal hiatus and lies next to: in frontal position, the trachea, the aortic arch and tracheal junction. The abdominal segment enters in frontal contact with the left hepatic lobe, at the median level with the caudal lobe, laterally with the gastric fornix and posteriorly with the diaphragm and aorta. At the level of the hiatus it connects to the diaphragm through the phren-oesophageal ligament (Leimer-Bertelli), which contains elastic fibres and collagen and is an anti-reflux element.

Arterial vascularization stems from the branches of the regions crossed by the esophagus: cervical from the inferior thyroid artery, thoracic from the intercostals, aorta, bronchial arteries, and abdominal from the left gastric region, the lower left phrenic and splenic regions. Venous drainage is insured in a similar way, for the upper segment by the upper vena cava, the medial by the azygous vena and the lower through the gastric veins.

Parasympathetic innervation is ensured by the direct vagus nerve or through the branches of the (lower) recurrent laryngeal nerve. At the thoracic level a plexus with sympathetic fibres emerges from the cervical sympathetic ganglia to which the vagus nerves also participate. In the lower third of the thoracic esophagus the vagal trunks are reconstructed, rotate clockwise and become the frontal vagus (the left), more variable insofar as position and ramification level are concerned, and the distal vagus (the right).

Lymphatic drainage does not have a segmental nature, which allows for rapid and extensive lymphatic metastases in the esophageal cancer. Also worth mentioning is the dissemination of the inferior thoracic esophageal neoplasm, including in the lymph nodes of the small curvature.

The mucosa is covered by a stratified and non-keratinous pavement-type epithelium continued by a cylindrical epithelium at the esogastrical junction. The border between these two epithelia is the Z line, which is important for the defining of the Barrett esophagus. The pavement cells contain glycogen which enables the presence of vital colorations necessary for differentiation from the metaplasic cylindrical epithelium. The sub-mucosa layer offers a certain durability to the sutures. The circular muscular tunica, more profound than the longitudinal one, is slightly thicker in the lower segment in achalasia. The external sheath is the adventitia, only the abdominal esophagus has a serous one.

Congenital malformations of the esophagus are normally diagnosed in the early stages, in newborns or infants, due to a suggestive clinical picture. These are: atresia, esotracheal fistula, stenosis and duplications.

PARACLINICAL INVESTIGATIONS include the radiological examination, esophagoscopy, manometry and pH-metry.

1. The radiological examination (barium enema) is the most convenient.

In general baritate paste is used, which has a progression starting from

deglutition and through to the stomach, the mobility and suppleness

of the esophageal walls can be followed by scopically or by

disorders of the esophagus, radiology supersedes endoscopy.

Examinations in double contrast, resulting from combination of

increases the accuracy of diagnosis. Suspicion of the presence of an

2. Esophagoscopy directly enables visualisation of the lesion and

collection of biopsies, cytological material and application of vital

3. Manometry is necessary in motility pathology where the catheter

registersand transmits data about spontaneous motor activity and

after deglutition (amplitude, duration and speed of the contractile

the contractile wave initiated by deglutition, which begins in the

upper esophagus and traverses the whole length of the esophagus.

Local stimuli (distensability, foreign bodies) initiate secondary

4. Esophageal pH-metry confirms the gastro-esophageal reflux. The

esophageal syndrome comprises functional signs of esophageal

paraclinical tests.

Esophageal pathology brings together a series of COMMON CLINICAL ELEMENTS, shared by all disorders on this digestive tract segment. The esophageal syndrome comprises: dysphagia, regurgitation, pain and sialorrhoea= excess salivation .

Dysphagia is the discomfort or the impossibility to swallow, disorder of the deglutition process which may occur to different degrees. Incomplete dysphagia manifests itself only for solids, as the patient swallows only semi-liquid and liquid food. When it is complete it is immediately followed by regurgitation. Progressive, continuous and rapid evolution towards the complete form defines esophageal cancer. Minimal dysphagia, as a discomfort with temporary pain, occurs in the initial stages of esophageal disorders. Paradoxal dysphagia manifested in the case of liquids and is absent in solids occurs in achalasia where it is intermittent and paroxistic, occurring in sudden outbursts interrupted by lull. It also evolves over an extended period of time without affecting the nutrition state. Persistent intense dysphagia, with sudden onset as a result of ingesting a chemical substance defines postcaustic or corosive oesophagitis.

Regurgitation can be defined as the involuntary retrograde flow into the oral cavity of certain foods ingested and undigested due to the fact that they could not reach the stomach. It occurs without effort and needs to be differentiated from coughing up or merycism (chewing and swallowing), when food has been swallowed past the cardia, this being a manifestation of certain psychological disorders. Regurgitation occurs with the dilation of an esophageal segment. The volume of regurgitation increases with increased dilation, being generally reduced in esophageal cancer and highly important in advanced achalasia.

Pain is variably located depending on the affected topographic esophageal region: cervical, dorsal, retrosternal and epigastric pain. Reflux-induced or caustic esophagitis causes intense pain. In the dilated segments stasis and secondary infection causes inflammations and ulcerations of the mucosa as well as persistent pain. Esophageal cancer is pain-free for extended periods, as the pain generally appears in advanced stages of surgical intervention.

Sialorrhoea (reflux of abundant salivary secretion from the oral cavity) occurs as a result of the esophageal stenosis process which disables deglutition of saliva and is accentuated by the high volume secreted through vagal reflex stimulation.

CORROSIVE ESOPHAGITIS

(POST-CAUSTIC)

Corrosive esophagitis is determined by the ingestion of caustic substances: acids, base substances or salts. Because of the easy access to packaged substances which are incorrectly deposited, accidental ingestion targets children in particular and occasionally inebriated adults. Cases of voluntary ingestion appear more frequently in adults, with the aim of achieving emotional blackmail or suicide.

Lesions depend on the chemical composition, quantity and concentration of the substance, as well as on the duration of contact with the mucosa.Strong acids produce a coagulation necrosis, impermeable to the subsequent action of the substance, therefore transmural necrosis occurs more rarely. The bases have a higher progressive penetration with a liquefying necrosis which can slowly cover the entire wall. Moreover, pain in contact with the oral cavity is more reduced for bases, which permits the ingestion of a higher quantity of substance. The contact duration also depends on anatomical factors, while the supracardial esophagus and the antropyloric area are usually the most affected.

The acute stage of the first four days is characterized by the presence of necrosis areas surrounded by an incipient inflammatory reaction. The granulation stage appears after elimination of the mucosa in the case of profound lesions, and lasts for three weeks. The transition towards the scarring phase is frequently followed by stenosis. These appear practically in all cases where the lesion has circumferentially destroyed the mucosa along its entire thickness. Laryngeal lesions need to be estimated through laryngoscopy, especially in patients with stridor.

CLINICAL PICTURE – This can be dominated by the state of shock determined by intense pain. Dysphagia, sialorrhea, odynophagia, possibly a hoarse voice, dyspnea or stridor complete the symptoms. At a later stage fever can occur and discharge of certain fragments of mucosa. Mediastinitis occurs in cases of perforation with septic fever, intense retrosternal pain and widening of the mediastinal shadow with pneumomediastinum. An objective exam identifies oral-pharyngeal lesions.

PARACLINICAL INVESTIGATION – The gastroscopic exam must be carried out in the early hours by an experimented specialist with an endoscope of reduced diameter. Examination must be interrupted when a necrosis area appears, as there is a high perforation risk. The advantage of an early endoscopic exam isthe possibility of placing a catheter for patients where there is an increased risk of stenosis. This device will serve in guiding the subsequent dilation manoeuvres. Repeating the endoscopic manoeuvres is recommended from week four onwards. It should be mentioned that there is always a correspondence between oropharyngeal, esophageal and gastric lesions.

DIAGNOSIS – is easily based on the patient history and the objective exam. Sampling the ingested and vomited liquid for forensic purposes is useful. The plain thoracic/abdominal x-ray exam evidences mediastinitis or peritonitis. A hydrosoluble iodating substance can be used as a contrast substance in suspicion of perforation. Barium is reserved for stenosis in order to estimate its localization and extension. Endoscopy enables a precise description of the lesions, with therapeutic and prognostic importance. GASTRO-ESOPHAGEAL REFLUX DISEASE (GERD)

Gastro-Esophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) is defined as the total number of symptoms produced by gastric reflux into the esophagus. Reflux esophagitis (RE) is not present in all subjects diagnosed with gastroesophageal reflux (GER) and implies the inflammatory modifications of the esophageal mucosa.

The incidence of GERD is higher in developed countries, possibly also due to the high consumption of carbonated drinks and a higher obesity rate. A great majority of patients which are treated for other conditions (chronic bronchitis, asthma etc.) are normally found to be suffering from less common forms of GERD.

A major role in the PATHOGENESIS of gastroesophageal reflux is held by the component elements of the esogastric junction complex:

  • The lower esophageal sphincter LES (internal sphincter);
  • The esophageal hiatus (external sphincter);
  • The phrenoesophageal ligament;
  • The abdominal esophagus;
  • The Hiss angle and mucosal folds on the gastric side of the esophageal gastric junction orifice (EGJ), the Gubaroff valve.

The lower esophageal sphincter is physiologically defined as a high pressure area of the esogastric junction, situated between positive intra-abdominal pressure and negative intra-thoracic pressure. During deglutition it functions as a valve which enables the flow only during exhalation, when the pressure gradient favours the flow towards the stomach. The normal pressure value at this level is 16 mmHg but it drops below 10 mmHg in gastroesophageal reflux.During exhalation the diaphragm pillars are relaxed and open, while during inhalation when abdominal pressure increases, the pillars become contracted and prevent gastroesophageal reflux. The phrenoesophageal ligament is one of the means of suspending the diaphragm, but also an elastic membrane-like system of fixing the terminal esophagus which isolates the esophageal hiatus between the diaphragm and the esophagus. The phrenoesophageal ligament, owing to its muscular fibres and together with the connective tissue, especially the elastic one, constitutes a fixing mechanism, both passive and active. It forms a system of elastic fixing of the distal part of the esophagus which enables but also limits the vertical passage of the esophagus relative to the diaphragm, and viceversa, of the diaphragm relativeto the esophagus during respiration, deglutition and postural changes.

The abdominal esophagus commonly measures between 1 and 2.5 cm. Preserving this length is essential for the prevention of gastroesophageal reflux through the sufficient surface on which the forces from two positive pressures are applied:

  • Intra-gastric, which tends to open the esophageal sphincter;
  • Intra-abdominal, responsible for the collapse of the esophagus with low internal pressure, after expulsion of the masticated alimentary bolus.

The abdominal esophagus approaches the stomach from a sharp angle known as the Hiss angle. Responsible for the maintenance of the cardio-tuberose angle are the smooth oblique muscle fascicles of the small curve which anchor the esogastric junction. The internal expression of the sharp Hiss angle is the submucous and mucous gastric ply (the Gubaroff valve), which isolates, similarly to a closing flap, the intra-gastric orifice of the esogastric junction, thus preventing gastroesophageal reflux.

Approximately 50% of patients with hiatal hernia (HH) have reflux pathology. Conversely, 90% of patients with gastroesophageal reflux pathology have hiatal hernia, demonstrating the close link between the two pathological entities, without perfectly overlapping. Hiatal hernia represents the abnormal protrusion of a portion of the stomach through the esophageal hiatus. Anatomically it is distinguished as follows (fig.1):

  • Type I – gliding hiatal hernia (axial), when the esogastric junction rises above the diaphragm;
  • Type II – rolling hiatal hernia (para-esophageal), with the esogastric junction beneath the diaphragm and the important tuberosity reached through lateral-esophageal hiatus;
  • Type III – cardio-esophageal malpositions.

In order to prevent reflux esophagitis an important role is played by esophageal clearance which is equipped with a double mechanism:

  • The major part of the reflux material is evacuated towards the stomach by the gravity gradient and owing to peristaltic contractions, thus constituting volume clearance;
  • A smaller quantity of acid, which remains in contact with the esophageal wall is chemically neutralised by the bicarbonates present in saliva – chemical clearance.

In gastroesophageal reflux disease pathogenesis, other factors are also responsible, besides the incompetence of the aforementioned anti-reflux mechanisms:

  • The rise of intra-abdominal pressure (pregnancy, obesity, coughing, ascites);
  • Surgical interventions on the stomach (upper polar gastrectomy, vagotomy, Heller operation, total gastrectomy with gastro-duodenal anastomosis);
  • Smoking, certain nutritional habits.

ESOPHAGEAL DIVERTICULI

Esophageal diverticuli are circumcised dilations at the level of the different portions of the esophagus, which communicate directly with the esophageal lumen.

1. CERVICAL DIVERTICULI

Cervical diverticuli described by Zenker represent 75% of the total esophageal ectasies. They appear more frequently in men over 60. PATHOGENESIS can be explained by a dissynergy of the cricopharingeal muscle which contracts prematurely, creating a pressure zone at pharingo-esophageal junction level. The distal wall has a thinner muscular tunica, which gives in progressively, making way for an orifice through which the mucosa and submucosa herniate. With gradual volume gain, the diverticulum becomes distal, lateral. The frequent association of this type of pulsing diverticulum with hiatal hernia has been demonstrated.

CLINICAL PICTURE: the main symptom, dysphagia, depends on the dimension, the filling degree and inflammation at diverticulum level. At liquid ingestion, a typical noise is made. Undigested foods, sometimes in putrefaction state, are regurgitated especially in right lateral decubitus. Stasis and decomposition determine foetor ex ore and appearance of diverticulitis.

POSITIVE DIAGNOSIS: Anamnestic data and discovery of a latero-cervical formation of variable volume, related to nutrition, impose running of a radiological exam with contrastive substance. Additional substance with rounded, regular contour is highlighted, with the neck on the median line and the lateral body projected on the left paravertebral region. Moreover, esophagoscopy permits the collection of biopsies, but presents the risk of perforation.

Secondary COMPLICATIONS of diverticulitis are: hemorrhage, perforation and after a prolonged, decade-long evolution, malignization. Through nocturnal aspiration of the contents, aspiration pneumonia can appear or lung abscesses. The compression of the recurrent nerve determines the appearance of the bi-tonal voice.

TREATMENT is surgical, with the exception of cases with mild symptoms or poor biological state. In orotracheal intubation, after dissection up to the diverticulum neck, the latter is resected and the esophageal wall is reconstructed by suture in two layers. In order to prevent recurrence, cricopharingeal myotomy is imperative.

2. PARABRONCHIAL DIVERTICULI

Parabronchial diverticuli appear in the retro-scarring retraction of a mediastinal lymph node adhering to the esophageal wall (in general after an infection with the Koch bacillus). It affects both men and women, especially in their late 40s. Traction diverticuli have a sharper form and a wall formed of all the normal esophageal layers. This type of diverticulum is frequently asymptomatic. Occasionally it triggers coughing fits, through adherence to the trachea or bronchia, or dysphagia due to associated diverticulitis. (Rare) complications are: hemorrhaging, perforation, pericarditis, pleuresia and esobronchial fistula. Symptomatic parabronchial diverticuli require surgical resection and suture in two layers. After resection and suture esobronchial fistulae impose the inter-posing of healthy tissues between the two segments in order to prevent recurrence.

3. EPIPHRENIC DIVERTICULI

Pulsing, epiphrenic diverticuli, are commonly localised immediately above the diaphragm and are due to esophageal dyskinesia. They are larger than the Zenker diverticuli and are frequently associated with achalasia and hiatal hernia. They can aggravate with the onset of diverticulitis, haemorrhage, perforations or even malignization.

CLINICAL PICTURE: epiphrenial diverticuli produce dysphagia and a pressing postprandial sensation at the lower esophagus level.These are associated with intermittent regurgitations and high epigastric pressure.

PARACLINICAL INVESTIGATIONS: the radiological exam with single and double contrast reveals the rounded, regular, slightly flattened contour towards the lower part of the diverticulum. The aspect is typical and esophagoscopy with biopsy is not necessary except for ruling out an incipient cancer overlapping with the diverticulitis process.

POSITIVE DIAGNOSIS:is suggested by dysphagia associated with severe, epigastric pains, which have a postprandial onset and which are alleviated after regurgitation.

TREATMENT: surgical treatment is indicated in cases with proximity compressions, dysphagia or regurgitation. Perforation is rare and constitutes an emergency indication. Approach though thoracotomy enables resection of the diverticulum and suture in double layers, with simultaneous settlement of any potential associated esophageal conditions (achalasia, hiatal hernia). The use of mechanic suture devices reduces the intervention time and the incidence of fistula.

ACHALASIA

(The Megaesophagus)

Achalasia (also improperly called a cardiospam) is characterized by the lack of cardia relaxation and lack of a well-coordinated peristaltic wave at the esophagus level.

PATHOGENESIS is insufficiently known. This functional disruption (dissynergism) is due to affected innervations of the esophagus with degeneration of the Auerbach plexus. The cause of degenerescence is unknown. Bacterial, viral infections, parasite infections (tripanosomiasis- the Chagas disease) and vitamin insufficiency have been incriminated. Recent experimental studies have highlighted as a possible cause the primary impairment of the trunk and the vagal nuclei. Achalasia targets the two sexes in equal proportions and has a maximum frequency in persons aged 30 to 50 years old.

CLINICAL PICTURE: it is usually suggestive. Dysphagia is the most constant and precocious symptom. At the onset it is intermittent, more accentuated in cold food than warm; it is paradoxical, transition being more rapid for solid foods than for liquid; it is paroxistic, appearing in episodes separated by lull. Over time, dysphagia becomes permanent. High or retrosternal epigastric pains are rare, define the incipient stages and are alleviated by the onset of esophageal dilation. Regurgitation is a usual symptom and appears more frequently at night, in clinostatism, leading to lung complications. It is more accentuated after the dilation of the esophagus. Sialorrhoea completes the clinical picture of achalasia.

EVOLUTION of achalasia is prolonged with progressive dilation of the esophagus and does not influence until late the nutrition state.

COMPLICATIONSare related to stasis esophagitis: ulcerations, haemorrhage and esophageal cancer (7 times more frequent). Aspiration of the esophageal contents into the respiratory tracts can determine aspiration pneumonia and lung abscesses.

PARACLINICAL INVESTIGATIONSare specific to esophageal conditions: of Achalasia (Megaesophagus)

(a)Barium swallow.Even in the incipient stages the lack of cardia

relaxation and superjacent dilation can be highlighted. Esophageal

peristaltism is uncoordinated or missing. Intravenous administration

of glucagon relaxes the cardia and is a necessary pharmacological test

for distinction from organic stenoses. During the evolution of the

disease the esophagus is dilated and defining images appear, with the

terminal portion narrowed into a cone, similar to a “radish” or a

“shell”. In the advanced stages, the esophagus is lengthened and

curved, appearing like a “sock”. The enormous dilations of the

esophagus can be highlighted even on the simple thoracic

radiography.

(b)Endoscopy in incipient achalasiaenables distinction from a benign

stenosis or heart cancer. With this aim, bioptic material is collected.

Esophagoscopy enables the recognition of stasis esophagitis with the

greatest accuracy. Manometry stages (persistent pressure of PES

over 25 mmHg) can confirm the clinical and radiological data.

Deglutition is followed by small, repeated and simultaneous

contractions, and by an uncoordinated contractile wave at the level

of the esophageal muscles. Pressure in repose at cardia level is

double by comparison to the normal state and relaxation is

incomplete in deglutition. Some patients present heavy contractions

at esophagus and cardia level. This data has enabled differentiation

of certain forms of hyper- or hypo-motile achalasia with complete

abolition of motility.

POSITIVE DIAGNOSISis relatively easy in typical cases. Intermittent, paradoxical and paroxystic dysphagia to which severe epigastric pains are added, regurgitation and sialorrhoea, prolonged evolution without affectation of the nutrition state are typical of achalasia. The radiological aspect and manometry data confirm the diagnosis.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISis carried out for:

  • Esophageal cancer which produces progressive dysphagia, has a rapid evolution and precociously affects the general state;
  • Epiphrenic diverticuli complicated by esophagitis can be distinguished based on the barium enema which evidences the rounded aspect with regular contour of the barium filling the diverticulum. Manometry in the diverticulum is normal, shaping the diagnosis is more difficult in cases of associating the epiphrenic diverticulum with the achalasia and hiatal hernia;
  • Hiatal hernia, difficult to distinguish clinically, requires barium enema in the Trendelenburg position and possibly, fibroscopy; manometry reveals low values of the lower esophageal sphincter tonus, by contrast to achalasia for which values are higher.

TREATMENT is conservative, based on avoiding stress, fractioned alimentation, avoiding foods that are too hot/too cold and administering of nitro-glycerine, amyl nitrate or nifedipin, has a limited effectiveness. Forced, mechanic, pneumatic or hydrostatic dilation has good results in approx. 65% of patients for a long period of time, but with perforations in 2% of cases. A special indication in this type of conservative treatment is represented by patients with surgical risk and recurrent achalasia after a Heller operation. If 2-3 sessions of dilations do not produce results, surgical intervention is required. The election procedure is extramucous esocardiomyotomy (Heller, 1913) which consists of performing a longitudinal incision of approx. 6-8 cm on the esogastric junction, with sectioning of the muscles reaching up to the mucosa.

Such procedures are often followed by reflux esophagitis, which is why today they are practically abandoned (exceptions are indicated).

BENIGN TUMORS OF THE ESOPHAGUS

Benign tumors may develop from any layer. Inflammatory polyps or granulomatous lesions associated with esophagitis may be considered neoplasms. Papillomas are usually small and are rarely large enough to cause obstruction. Sometimes they detach spontaneously and are naturally eliminated.

Leiomyoma is the most common benign lesion. It develops within the wall and the esophageal lumen is stenosed by extrinsic compression. The covering mucosa is usually intact, ulcerations occurring secondary to the pressure applied by a large tumor. Other benign tumors (fibroma, lipoma, myxoma) are rare.

Congenital cysts or esophageal dedoubling (second after leiomyoma as frequency) may occur at any level, more frequent in the lower esophagus.

The majority of benign lesions are asymptomatic. Large cysts and leiomyomas may be seen by simple X-ray. Esophageal stenosis appear benign, the disruption in the barium passage being spherical with a regular and clear contour. Peristalsis is not affected by leiomyoma, while congenital abnormalities are often associated with spasms of the adjacent segment. Dilations are rare.

Leiomyoma and malformation may be differentiated from esophageal cancer by contrast substance x-ray. Papillomas, polyps or granulomatous lesions can be differentiated from early neoplastic lesions only by biopsy. Biopsy of leiomyoma is negative if it is not deep enough and presents the risk of triggering intra-tumoral hemorrhage.

Cysts and doubled segments are supplied directly from the aorta, but bleeding risk is low, being associated with suprainfection. Periesophageal adhesions may cause dysphagia. Polyps with a long pedicle may twist and lead to infection, oedema and bleeding.

Bleeding is the most common complication of leiomyoma and occurs by ulceration of the covering mucosa. Small lesions may be resected endoscopically, but the intraparietal or malformed ones require surgery by cervical, thoracic or abdominal route.

Esophageal cancer represents 4-15% of digestive tract neoplasms. It is more frequent in Asia, in high alcohol consumption areas where also hot food and liquids are consumed. It is predominant in 45-65 years old men. Increased incidence is in patients with pre-existing esophageal lesions, stasis, caustic, peptic esophagitis, Barret’s syndrome (endobrachyesophagus) and Plummer-Vinson syndrome (caused by chronic iron deficiency, manifested by upper dysphagia, intermittent and not painful, caused by the trophicity of esophageal mucosa).

PATHOMORPHOLOGY of esophageal cancer generally shows a vegetative formation, sometimes with a central ulceration. Infiltrative, circumferential forms are often present, causing obstructive symptoms.

Microscopically the pavement carcinoma affects the cervical and thoracic esophagus, the abdominal one developing adenocarcinomas. Most pavement carcinomas are squamous cell carcinomas, the rest are basal cell one. The adenocarcionoma of the cardia extended to the esophagus is not included in the category, being classified with gastric cancer. Regardless of the type, esophageal cancers extend on the length under the mucosa, invade the esophageal wall and the neighboring tissues and disseminate through lymph and blood. In cervical locations the cervical lymph nodes are affected, especially the anterior jugular and supraclavicular groups. In thoracic locations, dissemination starts with mediastinal, supraclavicular and sometimes subdiaphragmatic lymph nodes. Lower locations give metastases to the celiac group and small gastric curvature nodes.

The upper two thirds rapidly invade the airways, large vessels, pleura, the thoracic outlet and the recurrent nerves. The presence of a mediastinal syndrome, eso-tracheal or eso-bronchial fistula, bitonal voice, Virchow-Troisier’s sign indicate that radical intervention is impossible.

Blood metastases affect the following, in this order: liver, lungs, bones. Esophageal sarcoma is very rare.

CLINICAL PICTURE includes three stages. During onset the dominant symptom is dysphagia. It starts slowly and progresses. It is a difficulty, very small at first, to swallow, with the feeling that solid food stops and a burning sensation at ingesting warm liquids. There is no strict correlation between the degree of obstruction and dysphagia. Endoscopic and cytologic studies carried out in China have shown the existence of an asymptomatic period of 3 years between evidence of cell dysplasia in the mucosa and the onset of a patent cancer with dysphagia. It is considered that dysphagia occurs with a 2/3 invasion of the esophagus circumference.

Pre-existing esophageal pathology (esophagitis, Barret and Plummer-Vinson) may mask an addition cancer. Late presentation to the doctor and considering dysphagia as a neurological disturbance mean great delays in the diagnosis and treatment.

In the status stage, dysphagia becomes permanent, first only for solids then also for liquids, at which time it is total. Accompanying signs, not constant, are: regurgitation, sialorrhoea, bad breath, hiccup, dysphonia etc. Pain is due to added spasms.

At the stage of COMPLICATIONS the following are present: aspiration pneumonia, eso-tracheal and eso-bronchial fistulas, mediastinitis and hemorrhage (very rarely by tumoral perforation of the aorta) At advanced stages, pain appears by the invasion of posterior mediatinum, pleura, vertebral periostium. The alteration of the general state due to weight loss, dehydration, asthenia and anorexia is impressive.

CLINICAL EXAMINATION. It is poor in the early, useful stage it may evidence a respiratory infection, supraclavicular adenopathy or liver metastases, all signs of advanced stage, when radical therapy is ruled out.

PARACLINICAL EXAMINATIONS are mandatory for the diagnosis.

Double contrast barium swallow, under various angles and administration of pharmacodynamic agents with effect on motility (amyl nitrite, glucagons) may be helpful for the diagnosis. Radiological images suggestive for esophageal cancer are:

  • irregular contour stenosis (apple core aspect);
  • eccentric stenosis with slight suprajacent dilation;
  • marginal emptiness;
  • niche.

They have the following features:

  • rigidity;
  • irregularity;
  • presence on all the images even after administration of pharmacodynamic agents.

Other aspects such as segmental rigidity, mucosal irregularities, pseudo-polypoid or extrinsic compression images prompt for further investigation.

Esophagoscopy with biopsy provides diagnostic certainty, confirms the radiological aspects and establishes the type (infiltrative, vegetative, ulcerated), site and histology of the tumor.

Screening campaigns carried out in Japan in large population groups allowed the early detection of esophageal cancer escaping x-ray examination. This does not do beyond the muscularis, and gangia invasion is rare. It accounts for 30-40% of the cases diagnosed in Japan, with 5 years survival postoperative rate up to 100%. Vital staining improves endoscopic efficiency in evidencing the early stages.

Endoesophageal ultrasound and CT scan combined with lymphography by endoscopic injection of the tumor establish the local extension, i.e. the tumor operability.

POSITIVE DIAGNOSIS of esophageal cancer is based on clinical, radiological and endoscopic methods. Late diagnosis, the main cause of low resectability, is due to the time interval of months between the appearance of dysphagia and presentation to the doctor, as well as the wrong interpretation of dysphagia as a functional disturbance. In principle any patient over 40 with dysphagia should be fully investigated. The typical clinical picture is a male patient, consumer of spirits, with progressive permanent dysphagia, for a long time without pain; the image of irregular eccentric stenosis with a slight dilation above also appears at barium examination. Esophagoscopy with multiple biopsies establishes the diagnosis.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS should be with other esophageal diseases.

Achalasia (mega-esophagus) is different from cancer by a paradoxical paroxystic intermittent dysphagia, with prolonged evolution; nutritional state is not impaired, important regurgitation occurs at advanced stages. Paraclinically barium enema provides the typical radish, missile or sock aspect, manometry evidences the marked tonus of the lower esophageal sphincter, and the fibroscope goes easily beyond the open cardia.

Asymptomatic diverticuli cause dysphagia, corresponding pain, bad breath and regurgitation followed by disappearance or minimization of pain and dysphagia. X-ray evidences a regular contour, rounded, lateral, outside the esophageal axis.

Benign stenoses may be suspicioned when patient has a history of post-caustic, reflux, infectious, drug-induced esophagitis, or radiation therapy of the chest. Differentiation by clinical criteria is often difficult, while barium meal evidences a stenosis of benign character: regular contour, axial, marked superjacent dilation. In all these cases endoscopy + biopsy establishes diagnosis, except cases of peptic and caustic stenoses in which biopsy is inconclusive, as there is a variable degree of dysplasia.

Extrinsic compressions of the esophagus should be ruled out, due to mediastinal adenopathy or tumors, retrosternal gout, vertebral osteophytosis, aortic aneurysm, pulmonary hydatid cyst.

PROGNOSIS of esophageal neoplasms is severe. In well developed countries postoperative mortality dropped under 10% for 60% operability and 30-60% resectability. 5 yearsurvival is 5%. Hope is based on targeting high risk population groups, following-up precancerous disorders (dysphagia, esophagitis) and detecting early or superficial forms of cancer.

TREATMENT of esophageal cancer is surgical. Depending on the stage of evolution, treatment may be radical or palliative. Preoperative care includes improvement of the general state, treatment of associated respiratory infections and preparation of the colon for a possible esophagoplasty.

Radical surgery consists of esophagectomy, replacing the excised esophagus with another GI segment. Partial esophagectomy, within oncological safety, is under scrutiny due to multifocal development (10-15%) of the esophageal cancer. The tendency is towards total esophagectomy. The approach differs according to location, the surgeon’s skill and technical equipment. Bipolar, cervical and abdominal approaches are preferred. More recently the thoracoscopic dissection of the esophagus is used. Keeping the chest “closed” avoids respiratory complications due to thoracic hypomotility.

The lack of the serosa and poor vascularization of the esophagus explains the frequent anastomotic leaks and fistulas that aggravate postoperative course. Subsequent mediastinitis and purulent pleurisy are fatal in 80% of the cases.

In case of radical surgery, neoplasms of the lower third require partial esophagectomy and upper polar gastric resection, 6-10 cm from the tumor. Cancer of the upper or middle third is removed by total esophagectomy. The radicality of the resection also involves removal of surrounding lymph nodes and lymph drainage. Digestive tube continuity is achieved by esophagoplasty. Among the most important methods are:

The techniques using the stomach and colon are more frequently applied and allow replacement of segments or even the whole esophagus. Palliative procedures are indicated in case of local and regional spread, as well as remote metastases. They aim at overcoming the obstacle in order to make possible feeding. A survival time of up to 18 months may be obtained. These methods are: surgery, radiation and chemotherapy.

Palliative procedures are:

  • palliative esophagectomy (with incomplete tumor removal);
  • endoscopic laser ablation of stenosing tumors by repeated outpatient sessions, entailing perforation risk;
  • transtumoral endoprosthesisindicated mainly in eso-tracheal fistula and lower esophageal stenosis;
  • alimentation gastrostomy performed surgically or endoscopically, difficult to tolerate from a mental point of view (it consists in establishing a communication between the gastric lumen and the exterior or through a Pezzer tube, allowing direct feeding).

Effective palliative radiotherapy especially in basal cell forms is indicated for:

  • completion of a palliative esophagectomy;
  • unresectable tumors;
  • local and regional recurrence.

The eso-bronchial fistula is a contraindication of radiotherapy. Radiation complications are: actinic lung, pericarditis and tumoral necrosis with eso-bronchial or eso-aortic fistula.

Chemotherapy, efficient in 20% of pavement carcinomas is applied preand postoperatively. The assessment of efficiency is based on a loco-regional examination after 2-3 months. The association of resection with radio- and chemotherapy has increased, clinical studies proving encouraging results. High-performance centers in Japan have a very promising activity in this respect.
